The Very Nearly Theory of Flavor

Abstract

A striking empirical observation about the CKM matrix is that the angles of the unitarity triangle (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) are very close to (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8), simple fractions of π\pi that are suggestive of an underlying theory linking flavor and spontaneous CP violation. However, relating this empirical observation to an underlying theory of flavor is challenging, since the unitarity triangle is a complicated function of the Yukawa matrices. In this letter we present a simple picture for the Yukawas where this direct link is possible. We begin by parametrizing the ten-dimensional space of flavor data via “nine-link textures”, full-rank Yu,dY_{u,d} matrices with a total of nine non-zero entries, with a single CP violating phase. Fitting the ten parameters of all such textures to the flavor data reveals a wonderful surprise: the CP phases cluster tightly around multiples of π/8\pi/8! This happens because the entries of Yu,dY_{u,d} naturally define a “Yukawa triangle”, in most cases identical to the unitarity triangle at leading order in small flavor parameters. Most interestingly, these two triangles are not the same beyond leading order, yielding precise predictions for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) with calculable deviation from (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8), which can be decisively excluded or strongly confirmed by the next generation of experimental measurements of the angles. The 9-link textures are sparse and their determinants are naturally real, which taken together with spontaneous CP violation can resolve the strong CP problem.

Seeking hidden patterns in flavor.—The origin of fermion flavor remains one of the deepest open questions in particle physics. While the Standard Model (SM) successfully describes quark masses and mixing through two Yukawa matrices, it offers no explanation for the striking hierarchies among quark masses, the hierarchical structure of the Cabibbo-Kobayashi-Maskawa Cabibbo 1963; Kobayashi and Maskawa 1973 (CKM) matrix, VV, or the origin of CP violation. Ultimately, the Yukawa matrices are expected to emerge from a more fundamental theory in the ultraviolet.

For decades, theorists have stared at the wealth of ever-more precisely measured flavor parameters, hoping to find simple and striking patterns that might provide vital clues to the origin of flavor in particular, and physics beyond the SM more generally – perhaps in the same way the recognition of the Balmer formula for the spectrum of Hydrogen augured the coming of quantum mechanics. Some qualitative relationships are clearly visible: for instance the hierarchies seen in the masses are also reflected in the mixings via the rough relation Vi​j∼mi/mjV_{ij}\sim\sqrt{m_{i}/m_{j}}. But beyond this evidence for what we might call “generic” hierarchical structure, very precise relations (as hoped for in the Balmer formula analogy!) have been much harder to come by. Perhaps the best-known simple relation is a much more accurate version of the generic hierarchy relationship, which holds for the first two generations via Vu​s≃md/msV_{us}\simeq\sqrt{m_{d}/m_{s}} Gatto et al. 1968; Weinberg 1977; Fritzsch 1977; Wilczek and Zee 1977; Wilczek and Zee 1979; Georgi and Jarlskog 1979, and the connection to texture-zero Yukawa matrices Fritzsch 1978; Wilczek and Zee 1977; Wilczek and Zee 1979; Fritzsch 1979; Georgi and Jarlskog 1979; Branco et al. 1989; Dimopoulos et al. 1992; Giudice 1992; Hall and Rasin 1993; Ramond et al. 1993; Ibanez and Ross 1994; Barbieri et al. 1997; Branco et al. 2000; Roberts et al. 2001. While these have provided valuable guidance in the search for organizing principles behind flavor, it is fair to say no class of theories have emerged as a compelling “canonical model of flavor”, and so the search continues.

In this letter, we report on what we believe is a truly remarkable pattern hidden in flavor, with possibly dramatic implications for various aspects of physics beyond the Standard Model, which also makes extremely precise experimental predictions that will be decisively confirmed or excluded by future flavor experiments. As an illustration, a compendium of our most precise predictions is shown in Fig. 3 11 1 Note that the predictions are sufficiently precise that the corresponding ellipses in the figure are hard to see. A later figure will zoom in on the regions I→IV{\rm I}\to{\rm IV} in the (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) plane populated by the predictions..

Our starting point is a different empirical observation about flavor, involving the angles of the famous “unitarity triangle”. Recall that this triangle is defined by the “d​bd\,b” entry of the unitarity relation for the CKM matrix Vu​d​Vu​b∗+Vc​d​Vc​b∗+Vt​d​Vt​b∗=0V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}+V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}+V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}=0; the angles of this triangle are then defined as

α=arg⁡[-​Vt​d​Vt​b∗Vu​d​Vu​b∗],β=arg⁡[-​Vc​d​Vc​b∗Vt​d​Vt​b∗],γ=arg⁡[-​Vu​d​Vu​b∗Vc​d​Vc​b∗].\alpha=\arg\!\left[\text{-}\frac{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}\right]\!,\,\beta=\arg\!\left[\text{-}\frac{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}\right]\!,\,\gamma=\arg\!\left[\text{-}\frac{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}\right]\!.

 (1)

Decades of exquisite measurements at BB factories have determined these angles with remarkable accuracy, yielding Takahashi et al. 2026

β=(22.6±0.5)∘,γ=(66.4−2.8+2.7)∘\beta=\bigl(22.6\pm 0.5\bigr)^{\circ}\,,\quad\gamma=\bigl(66.4^{+2.7}_{-2.8}\,\bigr)^{\circ}\, (2)

which when combined with the assumption of unitarity for the CKM matrix also determines

α=(91.0±2.8)∘.\alpha=\bigl(91.0\pm 2.8\bigr)^{\circ}\,. (3)

These precise measurements have in turn exposed a wonderful surprise: the angles of the unitarity triangle are not at all random, but lie remarkably close to simple fractions of π\pi,

α≃π/2,β≃π/8,γ≃3​π/8,\alpha\simeq\pi/2,\qquad\beta\simeq\pi/8,\qquad\gamma\simeq 3\pi/8, (4)

within current experimental precision.

These simple values are especially intriguing because discrete phases naturally arise in theories where CP is an exact symmetry of the Lagrangian and is broken spontaneously by the vacuum, which are in turn plausibly connected to theories for solving the strong CP problem.

It is then natural to ask: is the proximity of the measurements of (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) to (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8) merely an accident, or does it reflect a deeper structure connecting the physics of flavor and CP in the ultraviolet? A first indication that is encouraging for the pattern of angles “not being an accident” is the nice fact that (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) hardly run under the RG (see App. I.b), so whatever pattern we see at the weak scale is just the same as what we would see at the ultraviolet scale where flavor is generated.

But a moment’s reflection also makes it clear that connecting a striking pattern in the unitarity triangle to a deeper theory for the fundamental Yukawa matrices themselves should be challenging. There are many simple theoretical mechanisms – involving symmetries, anomalous dimensions, geography in extra dimensions, possibly combined with spontaneous CP violation – that can impose simple patterns at the level of the Yukawa matrices, which are, after all, the fundamental parameters in the theory. By contrast, the unitarity triangle itself is not directly reflected in the Lagrangian, and not simply related to the Yukawa matrices. The sides of the triangle are highly “processed” via diagonalizing the matrices, and are, in general, complicated algebraic functions of the entries of the Yukawa matrices. Thus it appears unlikely that some sort of “simplicity” at the level of the Yukawas could be directly connected to “simplicity” at the level of the unitarity triangle, and vice-versa.

This is the central surprise of our work: there is a picture for the Yukawa matrices, where the “highly processed” unitarity triangle is in fact directly reflected in very simple properties of the matrices.

We consider full-rank Yu,dY_{u,d} matrices with a total of nine zeros and a single rephasing invariant – these can be represented pictorially with “link-diagrams” (see Fig. 2, left), with nodes representing the fields and links denoting the non-zero entries, which are placed such that there is a single closed loop, associated with the CP violating phase. We will see that in some cases the links in this closed loop themselves naturally define two sides of a triangle, the “Yukawa triangle”, which at leading order in small flavor parameters, is the same as the unitarity triangle! Thus simple assumptions about this “Yukawa triangle” make predictions about the unitarity triangle. For example, we can demand that only one of the angles of this triangle is (depending on the texture) (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8) and that leads to a prediction for the corresponding angle in the unitarity triangle. Or we can demand further that the angles of the Yukawa triangle are exactly (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8) and this predicts the full unitarity triangle (see Fig. 2, right). But most interestingly and importantly, the correspondence between the “Yukawa triangle” and the “unitarity triangle” is not exact beyond leading order in small flavor parameters, but has precisely calculable corrections. Thus, the demanding “simplicity” in the angles of the Yukawa triangles, leads to very precisely calculable deviations from these special values in the actual unitarity triangle!

We find this particularly exciting, because the next generation of flavor measurements at Belle II and LHCb are slated to improve the experimental errors on the angles by nearly an order of magnitude Altmannshofer et al. 2019; Aaij et al. 2018; ATL 2025; LHC 2021; Vagnoni 2025. In Fig. 2 we illustrate an example of the precise predictions from one texture, also indicating the projected future error bars – making clear how future sensitivities will play a decisive role in either ruling out or confirming these predictions. As we will see in the rest of this letter, this conclusion extends to considering the predictions of all possible nine link textures, whose more systematic description we turn to now.

Parametrizing flavor with 9-link textures.— Amusingly, we were led to our results not by directly thinking about connections between the unitarity triangle and the Yukawas, but rather by looking for an invariant way of parametrizing the flavor data. In this representation, the data naturally reveals the surprise that makes our subsequent theory for the unitarity angles possible. We believe this way of looking at flavor is of independent general interest and deserves further attention beyond the implications for the unitarity triangle.

As we have recalled, the connection between flavor observables and the fundamental Yukawa matrices is highly non-unique. The 3×33\times 3 Yukawa matrices, Yu,dY_{u,d}, have 2×32×2=362\times 3^{2}\times 2=36 real degrees of freedom, while there are only 10 flavor observables. Of course, all those Yu,dY_{u,d} matrices that are related by the U​(3)3=U​(3)Q×U​(3)uc×U​(3)dcU(3)^{3}=U(3)_{Q}\times U(3)_{u^{c}}\times U(3)_{d^{c}} flavor symmetries are physically indistinguishable in the low-energy effective theory of the SM. Thus flavor space is really 36−3×32+1=1036-3\times 3^{2}+1=10 dimensional, and the most physical way to parametrize the equivalence class of all matrices up to the action of U​(3)3U(3)^{3} is to specify the 10 flavor parameters contained in the 6 eigenvalues, 3 angles, and 1 phase in the CKM matrix. While this parametrization of flavor is completely physical and invariant, it is not directly useful to the flavor model-builder, for whom the full 36-dimensional space is meaningful. This is because UV theories of flavor introduce more fields and new dynamics that break the U⁡(3)U(3) symmetries, so different forms of Yu,dY_{u,d} suggest inequivalent UV origins for flavor.

It is then natural to ask: can we parametrize the flavor data directly in terms of quark Yukawa matrices Yu​(li),Yd​(li)Y_{u}(l_{i}),Y_{d}(l_{i}) depending on only ten parameters li=1,⋯10l_{i=1,\cdots 10}, so that the 10 masses and mixings fix the lil_{i}? The most natural way of doing this is to set to zero as many entries of Yu,dY_{u,d} as needed to be left with the correct 10 d.o.f. – 99 entries and 11 phase, which precisely leads to the 9-link textures described above. Since the resulting Yukawa matrices are fairly sparse, it is convenient to represent them via the link diagrams, as in Fig. 2. By rephasing the fields (nodes), we can make every single link real and positive, except for one of the links in the closed loop – which must carry the rephasing-invariant CP violating phase, φ\varphi. Of course there are many combinatorial choices for where to place the zeros, so there are many parametrizations of this sort, which are by design all equivalent under U​(3)3U(3)^{3} rotations. Fitting the data to these 9 link textures gives us an alternative way of presenting the data of flavor in a way more transparently connected to the UV origin of flavor.

To cover the full parameter space, we perform a systematic scan over all 99-link textures, Yu,dY_{u,d}. For each texture, we fit the 99 real positive parameters and the CP phase, φ\varphi, to the 66 quark masses and 44 CKM parameters. Details of the scan and fitting procedure are given in SM. Among all textures, we find 156 different solutions, which are not related by trivial row/column permutations.

We then did the obvious exercise of making a histogram of the fit value of φ\varphi 44 4 throughout the text when we refer to φ\varphi we are always refering to the phase we get in the rephasing invariant up to complex conjugation as well as adding/subtracting π\pi.; naively one would expect this histogram to give us a featureless, uninteresting distribution. Surprisingly, as shown in Fig. 3, the result is completely different: the fit values of the rephasing-invariant cluster very tightly around a few values: (π/8,π/4,π/2,3​π/8)(\pi/8,\pi/4,\pi/2,3\pi/8)! It was then immediate to recognize (π/8,π/2,3​π/8)(\pi/8,\pi/2,3\pi/8) as the angles of the unitarity triangle, strongly suggesting that the triangle was directly reflected in the textures! The histogram also shows an interesting peak at φ∼π/4\varphi\sim\pi/4 which, as we explain in App. IV, reflects yet another pattern in flavor, not directly connected to the unitarity triangle!

Fixing the Yukawa rephasing invariant.— Taking the histogram seriously, it is natural to wonder whether we can still find a fit if we fix the rephasing invariant to be {π/2,π/8,3​π/8}\{\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8\} – which would let us predict {α,β,γ}\{\alpha,\beta,\gamma\}. Repeating the scan with fixed φ\varphi, we find, up to row/column permutations, 29 (π/2)(\pi/2), 35 (π/8)(\pi/8), and 35 (3​π/8)(3\pi/8) 9-link textures yielding fits with χ2\chi^{2} values below the 3​σ3\,\sigma confidence-level threshold. We show the link-diagrams for all these classes in App. V. In the full scan, for a given texture we find different fits, corresponding to different local minima. Most of these, however, do not exhibit a “hierarchical structure” – the left- and/or right-diagonalizing matrices contain large mixing angles and are therefore far from diagonal. Interestingly, within each permutation orbit there is at most one hierarchical fit, by which we mean that all diagonal entries of both the left- and right-diagonalizing matrices are ≥0.9\geq 0.9. For orbits in which this criterion cannot be fulfilled, there is nevertheless always one fit that is hierarchical on the left, but not on the right. In the rest of the text, we always choose the most hierarchical texture as a representative element of each equivalence class.

In addition to more transparently reflecting the data, having a hierarchical structure is practically useful as it allows for a controlled perturbative diagonalization, from which we can derive analytic approximations for the quark masses and the CKM matrix. Assuming this hierarchical structure of Yu,dY_{u,d}, in App.II, we give a general analytic derivation of the leading order predictions for α,β\alpha,\beta or γ\gamma. We find that if Yi​ju,dY^{u,d}_{ij} have phases that are multiples of π/8\pi/8, this translates into α,β\alpha,\beta or γ\gamma being a multiple of π/8\pi/8 only if there are texture zeros 55 5 Here, by “vanishing” we mean that the size of the entries are less than a percent of the “natural” hierarchical entries for the Yukawa matrix.! Hierarchical matrices can be approximately diagonalized by successive 2×22\times 2 unitary transformations, and the texture zeros enforce conditions on these transformations that are necessary for nailing the special values of the angles. We also show analytically that all realistic 9-link textures have φ\varphi close to a multiple (1,3,4)​π/8(1,3,4)\pi/8, φ\varphi is approximately (β,γ,α)(\beta,\gamma,\alpha), respectively.

Note, however, that once we fix φ\varphi, it is no longer guaranteed we can map any textures into each other using U​(3)3U(3)^{3} rotations – since these might not preserve φ\varphi. Modding-out by those rotations that preserve the phase, defines the equivalence classes which lead to genuinely different physical predictions: 99 classes for φ=π/2\varphi=\pi/2; 1010 for φ=π/8\varphi=\pi/8 and 1313 for φ=3​π/8\varphi=3\pi/8. Applying perturbative diagonalization each class, we find as expected that in most cases, one of the CKM angles (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma), at leading order, is determined by φ\varphi! The only exception happens for three classes for φ=3​π/8\varphi=3\pi/8, where an accident between Yukawa entries ensures γ∼3​π/8\gamma\sim 3\pi/8, as discussed in App. V. Removing these three cases, we are left with (9,10,10)(9,10,10) classes for φ={π/2,π/8,3​π/8}\varphi=\{\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8\}, respectively.

Since these theories contain only nine independent real parameters, which are fit to the ten flavor observables, each class predicts one non-trivial relation among the CKM observables, which in this setting are the precise deviations from the exact values of α∼π/2\alpha\sim\pi/2, β∼π/8\beta\sim\pi/8 and γ∼3​π/8\gamma\sim 3\pi/8. In App. III, we show some examples of how the perturbative diagonalization of a 9-link texture lets us derive not only the leading contribution to each angle but also the precise sub-leading corrections, which can be fully recast in terms of the observables. In Fig. 4 we present the different theories (9,10,10) and their respective precise predictions for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma).

Our precise predictions arise from having as many zeros in Yu,dY_{u,d} as possible, but, obviously, these predictions can still hold to high accuracy as we deform away from 9-link textures. The analysis of App. II shows that texture zeros are still necessary for this to happen: there are many ways that textures and spontaneous CP violation can lead to one angle of the unitarity triangle being a (1,3,4)(1,3,4) multiple of π/8\pi/8 at leading order; but at least four zeros (and of course up to nine) appear in all patterns. Apart from this analytic understanding, a preliminary numerical study of these perturbations is also presented, confirming the many zeros that are needed to predict the angles close to the special fractions of π\pi. We leave a more systematic exploration of the deviations from 9-link textures to future work.

Fixing the Yukawa triangle.— So far we have focused on how we can control one of the angles of the unitarity triangle via the rephasing-invariant. For example, for α\alpha the relevant ratio is

−Vt​d​Vt​b∗Vu​d​Vu​b∗≡|Rα|​ei​α,-\frac{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}\equiv|R_{\alpha}|e^{i\alpha}, (5)

and in the π/2\pi/2-textures we find that the leading order expansion of these CKM entries are precisely such that the argument of the ratio is given by φ\varphi. Knowing that, at leading order, the unitarity triangle is a right triangle whose two orthogonal sides are Vt​d​Vt​b∗V_{td}V_{tb}^{*} and Vu​d​Vu​b∗V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}, it follows that β\beta is such that tan−1⁡(β)=|Rα|\tan^{-1}(\beta)=|R_{\alpha}|. By perturbatively diagonalizing the different textures, we find that in most cases not only α∼φ\alpha\sim\varphi, but also |Rα||R_{\alpha}| is precisely the rephasing-invariant monomial! For example, in class 44 of the π/2\pi/2 theories – the class presented in Fig.2 – we find that, at leading order,

Vt​d​Vt​b∗Vu​d​Vu​b∗∼D12U12,with ​D12=Y12dY22d,U12=Y12uY22u.\frac{V_{td}V^{*}_{tb}}{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}\sim\frac{D_{12}}{U_{12}},\quad\text{with }\,D_{12}=\frac{Y^{d}_{12}}{Y^{d}_{22}},\,\,U_{12}=\frac{Y^{u}_{12}}{Y^{u}_{22}}\,. (6)

Given that |U12||U_{12}| and |D12||D_{12}| are of the same order, it is then meaningful to think of the complex numbers, U12U_{12} and D12D_{12}, as defining the sides of a triangle – the Yukawa triangle (see Fig. 2). By fixing the argument of the ratio to be −π/2-\pi/2 we obtain a right triangle, but we can fully fix the triangle (up to rescalings) by further demanding

U12D12=i​tan⁡(π8).\frac{U_{12}}{D_{12}}=i\tan{\frac{\pi}{8}}\,. (7)

By construction we have that at leading order the unitarity triangle is exactly the Yukawa triangle, with angles (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8); and the subleading corrections are totally calculable!

Looking at the results of perturbative diagonalization for the different classes in Fig. 4, we find that the simplicity of RαR_{\alpha} described for class 44, is quite general, and generalizes to RβR_{\beta} and RγR_{\gamma} in the π/8\pi/8 and 3​π/83\pi/8 theories – in most cases the ratio is precisely the monomial in the rephasing invariant (see Tab. S3)! It is then natural to ask whether we can still fit the data by not only fixing φ\varphi, but the full Yukawa triangle. In the π/2\pi/2 case this corresponds to fixing the leading |Rα|=1/tan⁡(π/8)|R_{\alpha}|=1/\tan(\pi/8); for π/8\pi/8 and 3​π/83\pi/8 instead we have |Rβ|=1/cos⁡(π/8)|R_{\beta}|=1/\cos(\pi/8) and |Rγ|=cos⁡(3​π/8)|R_{\gamma}|=\cos(3\pi/8). In such a fit, we predict precisely two angles of the unitarity triangle, which assuming unitarity determines the full triangle. To do this analysis we go back to the (29,35,35)(29,35,35) hierarchical representatives of the permutation inequivalent textures (represented in Figs. S4-S6); and fix not only φ\varphi, but also the respective rephasing invariant monomial to {tan⁡(π/8),cos⁡(π/8),cos⁡(3​π/8)}\{\tan{\pi/8},\cos{\pi/8},\cos{3\pi/8}\}, respectively. Fitting to the data we find that (23,27,33)(23,27,33) yield fits with χ2\chi^{2} values below the 3​σ3\,\sigma confidence-level threshold. (see details in SM). As previously, to account for the textures which give physically different predictions we need to further mod-out by the subset of U​(3)3U(3)^{3} rotations which preserves not only the phase but the full rephasing invariant. In doing so we are left with (17,19,19)(17,19,19) different textures which yield extremely precise predictions for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) as shown already in Fig. 3. In Fig. 5, we present the zoom-ins on the different clusters of predictions, showing how small the 22-sigma ellipses are once we impose the constraint on the full Yukawa triangle.

Spontaneous CP violation and Strong CP.—As already remarked above, the simple fractions of π\pi seen in the unitarity triangle are suggestive of an underlying theory of spontaneous CP violation. Realizing these angles directly from simple phases in the Yukawa matrices cries out for this interpretation with much greater force.

There are several simple pictures for correlating the physics of flavor generation and spontaneous CP violation that can guarantee the entries in the Yukawa matrices have simple phases giving rise to our predictions. For instance, CP could be spontaneously broken by the vev of a complex scalar field, χ\chi, whose potential has a ℤ4\mathbb{Z}_{4} symmetry, giving rise to vevs that are purely real or purely imaginary – trivially guaranteeing that the phase in the “Yukawa triangle” is exactly π/2\pi/2. Similar ideas can be used to determine the full shape of the “Yukawa triangle” to match the (π/2,π/8,3​π/8)(\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8) triangle. For example, a combination of discrete and flavor symmetries can guarantee relations of the form Y12u,d=(χ1u,d+χ2u,d)​Y22u,dY^{u,d}_{12}=(\chi_{1}^{u,d}+\chi_{2}^{u,d})Y^{u,d}_{22} where the χ\chi’s get vevs respecting a ℤ8\mathbb{Z}_{8} global symmetry, thereby having equal magnitudes but phases that are multiples of π/4\pi/4. This can yield U12/D12=(Y12u/Y2,2u)/(Y12d/Y22d)=i⁡(1−ei​π/4)/(1+ei​π/4)=i​tan​(π/8)U_{12}/D_{12}=(Y^{u}_{12}/Y^{u}_{2,2})/(Y^{d}_{12}/Y^{d}_{22})=i(1-e^{i\pi/4})/(1+e^{i\pi/4})=i{\rm tan}(\pi/8). We defer a discussion of these theoretical possibilities to future work, as these are not directly relevant for the UV detail-independent, precise experimental predictions we wish to focus on in this letter.

But there is a final obvious point worth making in connection with spontaneous CP violation. As we have seen, the 9-link textures give Yu,dY_{u,d} matrices that are as sparse as possible to fit the data. These matrices have so many zeros, that with no special contrivance, in most cases, the simple phases can be placed in links such that their determinants are automatically real. The link-diagrams make it especially easy to see this: each term in the determinant is given by a perfect matching of the graph – a collection of edges touching all nodes exactly once. For example, in the texture in Fig. 2, there is a single term in Det(Yu​YdY_{u}Y_{d}), and therefore a single perfect matching for both the YuY_{u} and YdY_{d} matrices, which is

&\text{Det}(Y_{u})=Y^{u}_{11}Y^{u}_{22}Y^{u}_{33}\\ &\text{Det}(Y_{d})=Y^{d}_{12}Y^{d}_{21}Y^{d}_{33}\\ \end{aligned}\,. (8)

So if we place the phase in Y12uY^{u}_{12} or Y22dY^{d}_{22}, the determinant will remain real. As it turns out, almost all the 99-link textures have exactly this feature – there is a single perfect matching in YuY_{u} and YdY_{d}, and so one can always place the phase somewhere in the loop such that arg⁡(det⁡(Yu​Yd))=0\arg(\det(Y_u Y_d))=0. Out of the (29+35+35)(29+35+35) textures, only 55 fail this criterion (marked with (∗)(*) in Figs.S4-S6) – all 55 are diagonal in one of the sectors. Thus, for the vast majority of textures, having arg⁡(det⁡(Yu​Yd))=0\arg(\det(Y_u Y_d))=0 eliminates the Standard Model contributions to the QCD θ\theta angle, and suggests a full solution to the strong CP problem in the UV, with no appeal to axions.

Relation to previous work.— There is a vast literature on texture zero models for flavor, covering many patterns of zeros Fritzsch 1978; Wilczek and Zee 1977; Wilczek and Zee 1979; Fritzsch 1979; Georgi and Jarlskog 1979; Branco et al. 1989; Dimopoulos et al. 1992; Giudice 1992; Ramond et al. 1993; Hall and Rasin 1993; Ibanez and Ross 1994; Barbieri et al. 1997; Branco et al. 2000; Kuo et al. 1999; Chiu et al. 2000; Roberts et al. 2001; Xing and Zhao 2015, including those that emphasize 9-link textures as a canonical way of parameterizing flavor Branco et al. 2004; Ludl and Grimus 2015; Giraldo 2015; Emmanuel-Costa and González Felipe 2017. As we have emphasized, the central result motivating our work is an empirical surprise which, to our knowledge, had not been noted in previous literature – the striking clustering of the phase φ\varphi around multiples of π/8\pi/8 in scanning over all possible 9-link textures. There is also a related large literature on special choices of zeros and phases that can predict aspects of the unitarity triangle Masina and Savoy 2006a; Masina and Savoy 2006b; Xing 2009; Antusch et al. 2010; Harrison et al. 2009a; Harrison et al. 2009b; Antusch et al. 2011; Antusch et al. 2013; Mimura 2018. The relation between α≃π/2\alpha\simeq\pi/2, theories of spontaneous CP violation and the strong CP problem has also been emphasized Antusch et al. 2013. An especially interesting recent paper Harrison and Scott 2025 is also motivated by the same (α∼π/2,β∼π/8,γ∼3​π/8)(\alpha\sim\pi/2,\beta\sim\pi/8,\gamma\sim 3\pi/8) observation, which is used as motivation to consider a special pattern of Hermitian Yukawa matrices with two zeros each, and a constraint as in (7) – which yields a precise prediction for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) that differs from all of ours. More generally, much of the previous literature focuses on specific sets of textures (with various theoretical motivations), whereas we have focused on characterizing precise predictions for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) coming from all possible 9-link textures. It is striking that even taking all possible 9-link textures together covers only a minuscule fraction of the experimentally allowed space in (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma). We feel that these tiny islands furnish canonical “lampposts” in (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) space, which we can also perturb away from in a systematic way.

Outlook.— The current experimental determination of the unitarity triangle has put us in an extremely interesting position vis-a-vis the question of deeper structures underlying flavor. The measurements are suggestive of a striking pattern, but the error bars are still large enough to be consistent with nothing more than a coincidence. The order of magnitude reduction in error bars promised by the next generation of measurements thus carry enormous significance.

We find it fascinating that looking at the experimental flavor data through the lens of 9-link textures reveals a striking simplicity. Despite the great variety of these textures, the single irremovable phase is always determined to be close to a multiple of π/8\pi/8, strongly suggesting spontaneous CP violation and a solution to the strong CP problem, all in one fell swoop. This simple picture for flavor populates the allowed region in (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) space with miniscule islands having clean and direct theoretical interpretations. It is even more exciting that the extremely precise predictions for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) resulting from this picture can be decisively excluded or strongly confirmed by the planned level of precision of the next generation of measurements of these angles.

While we have focused on the sharpest predictions for the angles arising from 9-link textures, as we have mentioned, high-accuracy predictions for the angles with a few percent of their special values also hold when deforming away from nine-link textures, though still demanding four or more texture zeros. It will be very interesting to study these deformations more systematically, together with possible UV origins for textures leading to sharp predictions for (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma).

Indeed there are doubtless many more interesting theories of flavor that can give rise to other islands in (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) space. This state of affairs offers an important and exciting challenge for theorists to understand precise predictions for the unitarity triangle in the coming years, as we await the verdicts from experiment, and also a further inducement to experimentalists to try and make the most accurate possible measurements of these crucial observables.

I The CKM Matrix and the Unitarity Triangle

In the Standard Model (SM) the quark masses and flavor mixing arise from the Yukawa sector. After electroweak symmetry breaking by the Higgs vacuum expectation value vv, the quark mass matrices are Mu=v​Yu/2M_{u}=v\,Y_{u}/\sqrt{2}, Md=v​Yd/2M_{d}=v\,Y_{d}/\sqrt{2}, where Yu,dY_{u,d} are the 3×33\times 3 complex Yukawa matrices in generation space. Physical (mass) eigenstates are obtained by independent bi-unitary rotations,

M^u=VuLMuVu†R,M^d=VdLMdVd†R,\hat{M}_{u}=V^{u}_{L}\,M_{u}\,V^{u\,\dagger}_{R},\qquad\hat{M}_{d}=V^{d}_{L}\,M_{d}\,V^{d\,\dagger}_{R}, (S1)

where M^u=diag⁡(mu,mc,mt)\hat{M}_{u}=\mathrm{diag}(m_{u},m_{c},m_{t}) and M^d=diag⁡(md,ms,mb)\hat{M}_{d}=\mathrm{diag}(m_{d},m_{s},m_{b}) are real and positive, and VLu,VRu,VLd,VRd∈U⁡(3)V^{u}_{L},V^{u}_{R},V^{d}_{L},V^{d}_{R}\in U(3). In the SM, only the left-handed rotations are physical as they enter in the charged-current interactions through the coupling of the WW boson and combine into the observable CKM matrix Cabibbo 1963; Kobayashi and Maskawa 1973

V≡VuLVd†L.V\equiv V^{u}_{L}\,V^{d\,\dagger}_{L}. (S2)

The matrix VV is unitary by construction, V†​V=𝟏V^{\dagger}V=\mathbf{1}, and enters the charged-current Lagrangian as

ℒcc=g2​Wμ+​u¯L,i​γμ​Vi​j​dL,j+h.c.\mathcal{L}_{\rm cc}=\frac{g}{\sqrt{2}}\,W_{\mu}^{+}\,\bar{u}_{L,i}\,\gamma^{\mu}\,V_{ij}\,d_{L,j}+\mathrm{h.c.} (S3)

A 3×33\times 3 unitary matrix has nine real parameters; five independent quark-field rephasing freedoms remove five phases, leaving four physical parameters: three real mixing angles and one CP-violating phase δ\delta. The unique rephasing-invariant measure of CP violation is the Jarlskog invariant Jarlskog 1985, JJ,

J​∑m,nϵi​j​m​ϵk​l​n=Im⁡(Vi​j​Vk​l​Vi​l∗​Vk​j∗),J\sum_{m,n}\epsilon_{ijm}\epsilon_{kln}=\mathrm{Im}\!\left(V_{ij}V_{kl}V_{il}^{*}V_{kj}^{*}\right), (S4)

which vanishes if and only if CP is conserved in the quark sector. Experimentally, J≃3.12×10−5J\simeq 3.12\times 10^{-5} Navas et al. 2024, and therefore CP is violated by the weak interactions.

The unitarity of VV implies six off-diagonal orthogonality conditions. The relation involving the first and third columns,

Vu​d​Vu​b∗+Vc​d​Vc​b∗+Vt​d​Vt​b∗=0,V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}+V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}+V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}=0, (S5)

defines a triangle in the complex plane, one of six such triangles implied by unitarity. All six have the same area J/2J/2, and therefore encode identical information about CP violation. However, measuring this area experimentally requires 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) interior angles; for the other five triangles one side is much shorter than the remaining two, and so the triangle is very squashed and the associated CP asymmetries in meson decays are suppressed. The triangle of Eq. (S5) – the unitarity triangle (UT) – has all three sides of comparable magnitude Navas et al. 2024, |Vu​d​Vu​b∗|≃3.6×10−3\left|V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}\right|\simeq 3.6\times 10^{-3}, |Vc​d​Vc​b∗|≃9.4×10−3\left|V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}\right|\simeq 9.4\times 10^{-3}, and so all three angles are 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) and the area J/2J/2 is directly accessible through BB-meson decay asymmetries. Dividing Eq. (S5) by Vc​d​Vc​b∗V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*} and normalizing the base to unity, the three interior angles are defined as Navas et al. 2024

α=arg⁡[-​Vt​d​Vt​b∗Vu​d​Vu​b∗],β=arg⁡[-​Vc​d​Vc​b∗Vt​d​Vt​b∗],γ=arg⁡[-​Vu​d​Vu​b∗Vc​d​Vc​b∗],\alpha=\arg\!\left[\text{-}\frac{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}\right]\!,\quad\quad\beta=\arg\!\left[\text{-}\frac{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}\right]\!,\quad\quad\gamma=\arg\!\left[\text{-}\frac{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}\right]\!, (S6)

satisfying α+β+γ=π\alpha+\beta+\gamma=\pi.

I.a Experimental determination of α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma

The angle β\beta is the most precisely determined angle of the unitarity triangle, through time-dependent CP asymmetries in b→c​c¯​sb\to c\bar{c}s transitions 66 6 There is a four-fold ambiguity in the extraction of β\beta from determinations of sin⁡(2​β)\sin(2\beta) that can be resolved by the measurement of cos⁡(2​β)\cos(2\beta) and by a global fit Charles et al. 2005; Bona et al. 2005.. The angle γ\gamma is instead extracted from time-dependent CP asymmetries in B→D​KB\to DK processes. Statistical combinations of several decay channels lead to the results Takahashi et al. 2026

β=(22.6±0.5)∘,γ=(66.4−2.8+2.7)∘.\beta=\bigl(22.6\pm 0.5\bigr)^{\circ}\,,\quad\gamma=\bigl(66.4^{+2.7}_{-2.8}\bigr)^{\circ}\,. (S7)

The angle α\alpha can be directly accessed only through b→u​u¯​db\to u\bar{u}d transitions. The determination is complicated by penguin amplitudes, which have a similar magnitude but a different phase than the tree-level contributions. To date, we have four independent determinations, from time-dependent CP asymmetries in B0→π​πB^{0}\to\pi\pi, B0→ρ​ρB^{0}\to\rho\rho, B0→ρ​πB^{0}\to\rho\pi and B0→a1​πB^{0}\to a_{1}\pi decays. The world averages per decay channel obtained by Ref. Amhis et al. 2023 are

B0→π​π:(84.8−5.6+22.1)∘∪(99.6−20.4+7.3)∘,B0→ρ​ρ:(91.0±5.5)∘,B0→ρ​π:(53.4−11.1+8.3)∘,B0→a1​π:(79±7±11)∘.\begin{aligned} B^{0}\to\pi\pi\,:&\quad(84.8^{+22.1}_{-5.6})^{\circ}\cup(99.6^{+7.3}_{-20.4})^{\circ}\,,\\ B^{0}\to\rho\rho\,:&\quad(91.0\pm 5.5)^{\circ}\,,\\ \end{aligned}\quad\quad\quad\quad\begin{aligned} B^{0}\to\rho\pi\,:&\quad(53.4^{+8.3}_{-11.1})^{\circ}\,,\\ B^{0}\to a_{1}\pi\,:&\quad(79\pm 7\pm 11)^{\circ}\,.\end{aligned} (S8)

Combining these measurements, Ref. Takahashi et al. 2026 obtains a world average of

α=(84.1)−3.0+3.7∘.\alpha=\bigl(84.1\,{}^{+3.7}_{-3.0}\bigr)^{\circ}\,. (S9)

For more details and results obtained with different statistical treatments we refer the reader to Refs. Amhis et al. 2023; Charles et al. 2017.
An alternative way to determine α\alpha, is through the unitarity condition in Eq. S5, from the measurement of the angles β\beta and γ\gamma. Using these result and the unitarity of the CKM matrix, we obtain

αUT=(91.0)−2.8+2.8∘.\alpha^{\rm UT}=\bigl(91.0\,{}^{+2.8}_{-2.8}\bigr)^{\circ}\,. (S10)

Finally, a third determination of α\alpha can be obtained by a global fit of the CKM matrix. To the best of our knowledge, some of the most recent results are:

 CKMfitter CKM 2025:α=(90.82)−0.82+1.56∘, UTfit UTf 2025:α=(91.7±+1.3)∘.\text{ CKMfitter~\cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{CKMfitter2025}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}}:\quad\alpha=\bigl(90.82\,{}^{+1.56}_{-0.82}\bigr)^{\circ}\,,\quad\quad\quad\text{ UTfit~\cite[cite]{\@@bibref{Authors Phrase1YearPhrase2}{UTfit2025}{\@@citephrase{(}}{\@@citephrase{)}}}}:\quad\alpha=\bigl(91.7\,\pm{+1.3}\bigr)^{\circ}\,. (S11)

Although the direct measurements of α\alpha, β\beta, and γ\gamma are not perfectly compatible with CKM unitarity, our fits impose exact unitarity of the CKM matrix. Consequently, the fitted angles represent the values that best accommodate the direct measurements under the unitarity constraint. In the future, the Belle II and the LHCb experiment are expected to notably improve on the measurements of α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma. Tab. S1 shows projected sensitivities with data samples that will be recorded by early 2030s and 2040s.

I.b Renormalization Group Running of the CKM Matrix

In the main text, we argue on the significance of the close proximity of the angles of the unitarity triangle to simple fractions of π\pi as a hint for some underlying structure in the Yukawa matrices connected to some UV origin of flavor. However, if there is such a UV explanation it would only determine the angles at the UV scale, Λf\Lambda_{f}, where flavor is generated. It is therefore important to understand the scale dependence of (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma). If the RG scaling in the angles was significant, this would force Λf\Lambda_{f} to be very close to the weak-scale. But very nicely, as we now show, the opposite is true – (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) barely run at all, and thus the angles we measure in the IR are reflecting what is determined in the UV to extremely high accuracy, well beneath current and future error bars.

We work in the MS¯\overline{\rm MS} scheme. Let us define

ξu=YuYu†,ξd=YdYd†, with eigenstates ξu|ui⟩=yui2|ui⟩,ξd|di⟩=ydi2|di⟩,\xi_{u}=Y_{u}Y_{u}^{\dagger},\quad\xi_{d}=Y_{d}Y_{d}^{\dagger},\quad\text{ with eigenstates }\quad\xi_{u}\ket{u_i}=y_{u_{i}}^{2}\ket{u_i},\,\xi_{d}\ket{d_i}=y_{d_{i}}^{2}\ket{d_i}\,, (S12)

so that VLu,dV_{L}^{u,d} are the diagonalizing matrices of ξu,d\xi_{u,d}; and the CKM matrix, VV in (S2), can be equivalently given as V≡⟨ui|​|dj⟩V\equiv\bra{u_i}\ket{d_j}. To obtain the RGE of the unitarity angles we start by deriving the RGE for the full CKM:

V˙ui,dj=⟨u˙i|dj⟩+⟨ui|d˙j⟩,\dot{V}_{u_{i},d_{j}}=\langle\dot{u}_{i}|d_{j}\rangle+\langle u_{i}|\dot{d}_{j}\rangle\,, (S13)

where a dot denotes d/d​ln⁡μd/d\ln\mu. From first order perturbation theory in quantum mechanics, we know that for any hermitian operator, 𝒪⁡(μ)\mathcal{O}(\mu), with eigenvectors, |ψ˙​(μ)⟩|\dot{\psi}(\mu)\rangle and eigenvalues λ⁡(μ)\lambda(\mu); we can find the μ\mu-dependence of |ψ˙​(μ)⟩|\dot{\psi}(\mu)\rangle in terms of the μ\mu-dependence of 𝒪\mathcal{O} as follows:

|ψ˙​(μ)⟩=∑ψ′≠ψ|ψ′​(μ)⟩​⟨ψ′​(μ)|𝒪˙​(μ)|ψ⁡(μ)⟩(λ⁡(μ)−λ′​(μ))+c⁡(μ)​|ψ⁡(μ)⟩,|\dot{\psi}(\mu)\rangle=\sum_{\psi^{\prime}\neq\psi}\frac{|\psi^{\prime}(\mu)\rangle\langle\psi^{\prime}(\mu)|\dot{\mathcal{O}}(\mu)|\psi(\mu)\rangle}{(\lambda(\mu)-\lambda^{\prime}(\mu))}+c(\mu)|\psi(\mu)\rangle, (S14)

where since ⟨ψ|ψ⟩=1⇔⟨ψ˙|ψ⟩+⟨ψ|ψ˙⟩=0\bra{\psi}\ket{\psi}=1\Leftrightarrow\langle\dot{\psi}|\psi\rangle+\langle\psi|\dot{\psi}\rangle=0, and therefore we have that c⁡(μ)c(\mu) is purely imaginary, and so we can always rephase ψ\psi to remove c⁡(μ)c(\mu). As a result, in our case this yields

|u˙i⟩=∑k≠i|uk⟩​⟨uk|ξ˙u|ui⟩yui2−yuk2,|d˙j⟩=∑k≠j|dk⟩​⟨dk|ξ˙d|dj⟩ydj2−ydk2.|\dot{u}_{i}\rangle=\sum_{k\neq i}\frac{|u_{k}\rangle\langle u_{k}|\dot{\xi}_{u}|u_{i}\rangle}{y_{u_{i}}^{2}-y^{2}_{u_{k}}}\,,\quad\quad|\dot{d}_{j}\rangle=\sum_{k\neq j}\frac{|d_{k}\rangle\langle d_{k}|\dot{\xi}_{d}|d_{j}\rangle}{y_{d_{j}}^{2}-y^{2}_{d_{k}}}. (S15)

From the one-loop running of the Yukawa matrices in the SM, we have

16​π2​Y˙u=αu​Yu+βu​Yu​Yu†​Yu+γu​Yd​Yd†​Yu,⇒16​π2​ξ˙u=(αu+αu∗)​ξu+(βu+βu∗)​ξu2+(γu​ξd​ξu+h.c.),16\pi^{2}\dot{Y}_{u}=\alpha_{u}Y_{u}+\beta_{u}Y_{u}Y_{u}^{\dagger}Y_{u}+\gamma_{u}Y_{d}Y_{d}^{\dagger}Y_{u},\quad\Rightarrow\quad 16\pi^{2}\dot{\xi}_{u}=(\alpha_{u}+\alpha^{*}_{u})\xi_{u}+(\beta_{u}+\beta^{*}_{u})\xi_{u}^{2}+(\gamma_{u}\xi_{d}\xi_{u}+\text{h.c.}), (S16)

and similar for the down sector. So the only 1-loop contribution which leads to a non-vanishing contribution to (S15) is then the γu,d\gamma_{u,d} piece. Plugging it back into (S13), we find the following 1-loop RG equation for the CKM matrix:

16​π2​V˙i,j=γu​∑l∑k≠iri,ku​λdl2​Vi,l​Vk,l∗​Vk,j+γd​∑l∑k≠jrj,kd​λdl2​Vi,k​Vl,k∗​Vl,j, with ​ri,k=yi2+yk2yi2−yk2,16\pi^{2}\dot{V}_{i,j}=\gamma_{u}\sum_{l}\sum_{k\neq i}r^{u}_{i,k}\lambda_{d_{l}}^{2}V_{i,l}V^{*}_{k,l}V_{k,j}+\gamma_{d}\sum_{l}\sum_{k\neq j}r^{d}_{j,k}\lambda_{d_{l}}^{2}V_{i,k}V^{*}_{l,k}V_{l,j},\quad\text{ with }r_{i,k}=\frac{y_{i}^{2}+y_{k}^{2}}{y_{i}^{2}-y_{k}^{2}}\,, (S17)

where γu,d=γ∗u,d=−3/2\gamma_{u,d}=\gamma^{*}_{u,d}=-3/2. From this, together with the definition of (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) in terms of the VV, as given in (S6), we can derive the 1-loop RG evolution for the angles – the results are shown in Fig. S1. As we can see, even up to the GUT scale, the angles change at most by ∼0.01%\sim 0.01\%! This is striking simply because the individual entries of VV run a non-negligible amount, but still the ratios defining the unitarity triangle remain almost invariant.

We can understand this result in a simple way analytically. Keeping the leading contribution to the RGE’s, it is very easy to see that, up to miniscule corrections, the sides of the unitarity triangle are rescaled uniformly under the RG, and thus the shape of the triangle (and hence the angles) does not change. The largest corrections to the RG come from the top Yukawa yty_{t}; the other corrections are already much smaller than current or projected future experimental bounds. Then, we have that

16​π2​V˙i,j=γd​∑k≠jrj,kd​yt2​Vi,k​V3,k∗​V3,j.16\pi^{2}\dot{V}_{i,j}=\gamma_{d}\sum_{k\neq j}r^{d}_{j,k}y_{t}^{2}\,V_{i,k}V^{*}_{3,k}V_{3,j}\,. (S18)

Since the down eigenvalues are hierarchical we can replace rj,kd→+1r^{d}_{j,k}\to+1 when j>kj>k and rj,kd→−1r^{d}_{j,k}\to-1 when j<kj<k. Hence, looking at the running of V1,3V_{1,3} and V3,1V_{3,1} that determine the unitarity triangle, we have

16​π2​V˙1,3=γd​yt2​∑k≠3V1,k​V3,k∗​V3,3×(+1)=−γd​yt2​V1,3​V3,3∗​V3,3,16\pi^{2}\dot{V}_{1,3}=\gamma_{d}\,y_{t}^{2}\sum_{k\neq 3}V_{1,k}V^{*}_{3,k}V_{3,3}\times(+1)=-\gamma_{d}y_{t}^{2}V_{1,3}V^{*}_{3,3}V_{3,3}\,, (S19)

where to get the second form we used unitarity of VV. Similarly we find

16​π2​V˙3,1=γd​yt2​∑k≠1V3,k​V3,k∗​V3,1×(−1)=−γd​yt2​(1−V3,1​V3,1∗)​V3,1.16\pi^{2}\dot{V}_{3,1}=\gamma_{d}\,y_{t}^{2}\sum_{k\neq 1}V_{3,k}V^{*}_{3,k}V_{3,1}\times(-1)=-\gamma_{d}y_{t}^{2}(1-V_{3,1}V^{*}_{3,1})V_{3,1}\,. (S20)

Since |V3,3|2|V_{3,3}|^{2} and (1−|V3,1|2)(1-|V_{3,1}|^{2}) are both incredibly close to 1, we find that to leading order

16​π2​V˙1,3=−γd​yt2​V1,3, 16​π2​V˙3,1=−γd​yt2​V3,116\pi^{2}\dot{V}_{1,3}=-\gamma_{d}y_{t}^{2}V_{1,3},\quad\quad\,16\pi^{2}\dot{V}_{3,1}=-\gamma_{d}y_{t}^{2}V_{3,1} (S21)

which tells us that at leading order, the sides of the unitarity triangle are rescaled by exactly the same factor under the RG, hence the angles remain fixed.

II Approximate Analytic Predictions for α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma from Texture Zeros

We start by considering some underlying theory of flavor where all entries of YU,DY^{U,D} are non-zero and complex. In general α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma will have a complicated dependence on the 10 phases that cannot be removed by field redefinitions. In view of the experimental observation that α≃π/2,\alpha\simeq\pi/2,, β≃π/8,\beta\simeq\pi/8, and γ≃3​π/8\gamma\simeq 3\pi/8, are there any simple constraints on the theory that force α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma close to multiples of π/8\pi/8? We assume that the small dimensionless numbers observed in quark mass ratios and the CKM matrix are accounted for by Yu,dY_{u,d} taking a hierarchical form

|Yi​ju,d|≪|Yk​lu,d|,i+j<k+l.|Y^{u,d}_{ij}|\ll|Y^{u,d}_{kl}|,\qquad i+j<k+l. (S22)

This still leaves great ambiguity in the magnitudes of the various elements and, on occasions, it is useful to have a more definite standard hierarchical form. We use a form governed by an approximate U​(1)9U(1)^{9} flavor symmetry Carrasco-Martinez and Hall 2026, with one U(1) and one real spurion, ϵiq,uc,dc\epsilon^{q,u^{c},d^{c}}_{i}, for each of the 9 Weyl quark fields, giving

Yi​ju=Ci​ju​ϵiq​ϵjuc,Yi​jd=Ci​jd​ϵiq​ϵjdc.Y^{u}_{ij}\;=\;C^{u}_{ij}\,\epsilon^{q}_{i}\epsilon^{u^{c}}_{j},\hskip 14.45377ptY^{d}_{ij}\;=\;C^{d}_{ij}\,\epsilon^{q}_{i}\epsilon^{d^{c}}_{j}. (S23)

Fitting to the quark masses and mixing angles, ϵiq,uc,dc\epsilon^{q,u^{c},d^{c}}_{i} are chosen so that Ci​ju,dC^{u,d}_{ij} have order unity magnitudes and arbitrary phases. A texture zero occurs in Yi​ju,dY^{u,d}_{ij} if |Ci​ju,d|≪1|C^{u,d}_{ij}|\ll 1.
In a 2-generation model, Yu,dY_{u,d} can be diagonalized exactly by small-angle bi-unitary transformations, giving the CKM matrix V=VuLVd†LV=V^{u}_{L}V^{d\,\dagger}_{L} with

VLu,d=(cs−s∗c)u,d=[P∗​(c|s|−|s|c)​P]u,d;su,d=|s|u,d​ei​ϕu,d,cu,d=1−(|s|2)u,d,V^{u,d}_{L}=\begin{pmatrix}c&s\\ -s^{*}&c\end{pmatrix}^{u,d}=\left[P^{*}\begin{pmatrix}c&|s|\\ -|s|&c\end{pmatrix}P\right]^{u,d};\qquad s^{u,d}=|s|^{u,d}\;e^{i\phi^{u,d}},\;\;c^{u,d}=\sqrt{1-(|s|^{2})^{u,d}}, (S24)

where Pu,dP^{u,d} is a diagonal phase matrix Diag(ei​ϕu,d,1)(e^{i\phi^{u,d}},1) and

(S25)

With three generations, Yu,dY_{u,d} can be approximately diagonalized by successive small-angle 2×22\times 2 bi-unitary transformations; the CKM matrix is approximately

V≃Vu12Vu13Vu23Vd†23Vd†13Vd†12V\simeq V^{u}_{12}\;V^{u}_{13}\;V^{u}_{23}\;V^{d\dagger}_{23}\;V^{d\dagger}_{13}\;V^{d\dagger}_{12} (S26)

with

at leading order, giving

V≃(1s12s13+s12u​s23−s12∗1s23−s13∗−s12d∗s23∗−s23∗1),si​j=si​ju−si​jd.V\simeq\begin{pmatrix}1&s_{12}\;&s_{13}+s_{12}^{u}s_{23}\\ -s_{12}^{*}&1&s_{23}\\ -s_{13}^{*}-s_{12}^{d*}s_{23}^{*}\;&-s_{23}^{*}&1\end{pmatrix},\quad\quad s_{ij}=s^{u}_{ij}-s^{d}_{ij}. (S28)

Since |V13|≪|V12|,|V23||V_{13}|\ll|V_{12}|,|V_{23}|, we have ignored s13u,d​s23s_{13}^{u,d}s_{23} terms in V12,21V_{12,21} and s12u,d​s13s_{12}^{u,d}s_{13} terms in V23,32V_{23,32}. However, including these terms does not affect α\alpha. The key leading order predictions for α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma are

α≃arg​(s13∗+s12d∗s23∗s13∗+s12u∗s23∗),β≃arg​(sd∗12s23∗−su∗12s23∗s12d∗s23∗+s13∗),γ≃arg​(s13∗+s12u∗s23∗su∗12s23∗−sd∗12s23∗).\alpha\;\simeq\;\,\text{arg}\left(\frac{s_{13}^{*}+s_{12}^{d*}s_{23}^{*}}{s_{13}^{*}+s_{12}^{u*}s_{23}^{*}}\right),\qquad\beta\;\simeq\;\,\text{arg}\left(\frac{s^{d*}_{12}s_{23}^{*}-s^{u*}_{12}s_{23}^{*}}{s_{12}^{d*}s_{23}^{*}+s_{13}^{*}}\right),\qquad\gamma\;\simeq\;\,\text{arg}\left(\frac{s_{13}^{*}+s_{12}^{u*}s_{23}^{*}}{s^{u*}_{12}s_{23}^{*}-s^{d*}_{12}s_{23}^{*}}\right). (S29)

Inserting si​ju,ds_{ij}^{u,d} from (S27) gives α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma in terms of the Yukawa matrix elements.
In the absence of texture zeros, there is no reason for any angle of the unitarity triangle to be close to a multiple of π/8\pi/8. Using the hierarchical forms of (S23), corresponding to approximate U​(1)9U(1)^{9} flavor symmetry, s13s_{13}, s12d​s23s_{12}^{d}s_{23} and s12u​s23s_{12}^{u}s_{23} have comparable magnitudes of ϵ1q/ϵ3q\epsilon^{q}_{1}/\epsilon^{q}_{3}. Consider a theory where CP and flavor symmetries are spontaneously broken via the vevs of a set of flavon fields having phases that are multiples of π/8\pi/8. Further, assume that each entry in Yi​ju,dY^{u,d}_{ij} is dominated by products of these vevs so that, to leading order, each Yi​ju,dY^{u,d}_{ij} and each si​ju,ds^{u,d}_{ij} has a phase that is a multiple of π/8\pi/8. Could it be that, by choosing all terms in each numerator and denominator of (S29) to have the same phase, the ratios then predict angles of the unitarity triangle that are multiples of π/8\pi/8? The answer is no; the expressions for α,β\alpha,\beta and γ\gamma each have a common term in the numerator and denominator (s13,s12d​s23s_{13},s^{d}_{12}s_{23} and s12u​s23s^{u}_{12}s_{23} respectively), so that this procedure forces α,β,γ=0\alpha,\beta,\gamma=0.

For α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma to have a direct connection to the phases of the Yukawa matrix elements, the numerators and denominators of (S29) should not contain the same term. There are three extremely simple ways this can happen. Although there are six mixings, si​ju,ds^{u,d}_{ij}, the angles α,β\alpha,\beta and γ\gamma depend on only four combinations, s12u,s12d,s13s_{12}^{u},s_{12}^{d},s_{13} and s23s_{23}. While Vc​bV_{cb} requires s23≠0s_{23}\neq 0, one of s12u,s12d,s13s_{12}^{u},s_{12}^{d},s_{13} can vanish while still agreeing with data. Each of these three cases gives a greatly simplified expression for one of the angles of the unitarity triangle

α≃arg​(s12us12d),s13≃0;β≃arg​(−s13s12u​s23),s12d≃0;γ≃arg​(−s12d​s23s13),s12u≃0.\alpha\simeq\text{arg}\left(\frac{s_{12}^{u}}{s_{12}^{d}}\right),\;\;s_{13}\simeq 0;\qquad\beta\simeq\text{arg}\left(-\frac{s_{13}}{s_{12}^{u}s_{23}}\right),\;\;s_{12}^{d}\simeq 0;\qquad\gamma\simeq\text{arg}\left(-\frac{s_{12}^{d}s_{23}}{s_{13}}\right),\;\;s_{12}^{u}\simeq 0. (S30)

Thus, spontaneous CP violation leads to a natural explanation for why one of the unitarity triangle angles is a multiple of π/8\pi/8 if texture zeros force one of s12u,s12d,s13s_{12}^{u},s_{12}^{d},s_{13} to vanish. Furthermore, when the expressions in (S30) are written in terms of Yukawa matrix elements, using (S27), they should either be monomials in Yi​ju,dY^{u,d}_{ij} or, if there is a sum of terms, each term should have the same phase. For example, the two texture zeros |C13u,d|≪1|C^{u,d}_{13}|\ll 1 give

Y13u,d≃0,α≃arg​(Y22d−Y23d​Y32dY33dY12d​Y12uY22u−Y23u​Y32uY33u).Y^{u,d}_{13}\simeq 0,\qquad\alpha\;\simeq\;\,\text{arg}\left(\frac{Y^{d}_{22}-\frac{Y^{d}_{23}Y^{d}_{32}}{Y^{d}_{33}}}{Y^{d}_{12}}\;\frac{Y^{u}_{12}}{Y^{u}_{22}-\frac{Y^{u}_{23}Y^{u}_{32}}{Y^{u}_{33}}}\right). (S31)

If there are two further texture zeros from C32u,d≪1C^{u,d}_{32}\ll 1, then α\alpha is the argument of a monomial and, if spontaneous CP violation leads to each matrix element being dominantly real or imaginary, there is a 50% chance of α≃π/2\alpha\simeq\pi/2. The same result occurs without further texture zeros if Y22u,dY^{u,d}_{22} have the same phases as Y23u,d​Y32u,d/Y33u,dY^{u,d}_{23}Y^{u,d}_{32}/Y^{u,d}_{33}. Similarly, there are many possibilities for spontaneous CP violation to yield β≃π/8\beta\simeq\pi/8 or γ≃3​π/8\gamma\simeq 3\pi/8. In these cases, it may be more likely if the expressions in (S30) are monomials rather than sums of terms with the same phases. There are several different textures for each of these cases.

An alternative to (S30) arises if there are relations among various si​ju,ds^{u,d}_{ij}. Such relations occur when two Yi​jY_{ij} have a texture zero but both are generated by the same rotation on right-handed quark fields. For example, even with Y12,22d=0Y^{d}_{12,22}=0, Y32dY^{d}_{32} can generate sd12=−sd13/sd23s^{d}_{12}=-s^{d}_{13}/s^{d}_{23}. Substituting into (S29) for β\beta, and setting s23u=0s^{u}_{23}=0 by a texture zero, the numerators and denominators no longer contain the same term. A similar result occurs for γ\gamma when the relation is in the up sector, thus

β≃arg​(s13us12​s23d),s13d≃−s12d​s23d,s23u≃0;γ≃arg​(s12​s23us13d),s13u≃−s12u​s23u,s23d≃0.\beta\simeq\text{arg}\left(\frac{s^{u}_{13}}{s_{12}s^{d}_{23}}\right),\;\;s^{d}_{13}\simeq-s^{d}_{12}s^{d}_{23},\;s^{u}_{23}\simeq 0;\qquad\gamma\simeq\text{arg}\left(\frac{s_{12}s^{u}_{23}}{s^{d}_{13}}\right),\;\;s^{u}_{13}\simeq-s^{u}_{12}s^{u}_{23},\;s^{d}_{23}\simeq 0. (S32)

Either s13d≃−s12d​s23ds^{d}_{13}\simeq-s^{d}_{12}s^{d}_{23} or s13u≃−s12u​s23us^{u}_{13}\simeq-s^{u}_{12}s^{u}_{23} can lead to α\alpha not having identical terms in numerator and denominator, but only in the presence of two extra texture zeros

α≃arg(s23ds23u),s13u≃−s12us23u,s13d≃0,s12d≃0ors13d≃−s12ds23d,s13u≃0,s23u≃0.\alpha\simeq\text{arg}\left(\frac{s_{23}^{d}}{s_{23}^{u}}\right),\qquad s^{u}_{13}\simeq-s^{u}_{12}s^{u}_{23},\;s^{d}_{13}\simeq 0,\;s^{d}_{12}\simeq 0\qquad or\qquad s^{d}_{13}\simeq-s^{d}_{12}s^{d}_{23},\;s^{u}_{13}\simeq 0,\;s^{u}_{23}\simeq 0. (S33)

Thus, in general there are many ways that textures and spontaneous CP violation can lead to one angle of the unitarity triangle being a multiple of π/8\pi/8. However, such phase arguments cannot explain why a second angle also has this form. We conclude that (4) hints that CP is spontaneously broken in nature and that the Yukawa matrices have texture zeros, entries that are highly suppressed relative to expectations from approximate Abelian flavor symmetries. Future data could greatly strengthen this conclusion.

Even when texture zeros are present, there are several origins for deviations of α,β\alpha,\beta or γ\gamma from a multiple of π/8\pi/8. First, diagonalization by successive 2×22\times 2 transformations is approximate, so that there are corrections to (S26) and (S27). Most important for theories with Y13u,d=0Y^{u,d}_{13}=0, the transformations Y23u,dY^{u,d}_{23} of (S26) regenerate small but non-zero values of Y13u,dY^{u,d}_{13}. Also, the exact results for the phases ϕi​j\phi_{ij}, which take forms analogous to (S25), deviate from the leading result of arg​(Yi​j/Yj​j)\text{arg}(Y_{ij}/Y_{jj}). However, with U​(1)9U(1)^{9} approximate flavor symmetries these deviations are suppressed by mi/mjm_{i}/m_{j}, and are small. In general, none of these deviations can be predicted; even using U​(1)9U(1)^{9} as a guide, there are too many unknown parameters in Ci​ju,dC^{u,d}_{ij}. Hence, we now discuss the highly predictive set of theories with 9 texture zeros, the main subject of this paper.

Textures with 9 links have 9 real parameters and a single phase, φ\varphi. Six of the 9 real parameters are determined by the quark mass eigenvalues, leaving three to describe the six mixings |si​ju,d||s^{u,d}_{ij}|. In all 9-link textures some of these mixings are zero because of the texture zeros. Indeed, most have three of them zero, with the three that are non-zero chosen to fit the data. Requiring Vc​b≠0V_{cb}\neq 0 requires s23us^{u}_{23} or s23ds^{d}_{23} to be non-zero. There are three realistic possibilities for the other two non-zero mixings, one has both s12u,ds^{u,d}_{12} non-zero and s13=0s_{13}=0, while the others have one of s12u,ds^{u,d}_{12} non-zero and one of s13u,ds^{u,d}_{13} non-zero. Each possibility leads to a simple prediction for one of the angles of the unitarity triangle

α≃arg​(s12us12d),s13≃0;β≃arg​(−s13s12u​s23),s12d≃0;γ≃arg​(−s12d​s23s13),s12u≃0,\alpha\simeq\text{arg}\left(\frac{s_{12}^{u}}{s_{12}^{d}}\right),\;\;s_{13}\simeq 0;\qquad\beta\simeq\text{arg}\left(-\frac{s_{13}}{s_{12}^{u}s_{23}}\right),\;\;s_{12}^{d}\simeq 0;\qquad\gamma\simeq\text{arg}\left(-\frac{s_{12}^{d}s_{23}}{s_{13}}\right),\;\;s_{12}^{u}\simeq 0, (S34)

where, in the expressions for β\beta and γ\gamma, it is understood that only one of s13u,ds^{u,d}_{13} and one of s13u,ds^{u,d}_{13} are non-zero. These results have a close similarity with the more general result of (S30). A key difference is that, for the 9-link textures, one angle of the unitarity triangle is given by the phase φ\varphi, as the expressions involve the unique rephasing-invariant. All these textures lie in the φ=π/2,π/8\varphi=\pi/2,\pi/8 and 3​π/83\pi/8 peaks of Fig. 3.

There are also 9-link textures where 4 si​ju,ds^{u,d}_{ij} are non-zero. Since they are described by three free parameters only three are independent, so there is a relation between them. If Y12,22=0Y_{12,22}=0, a rotation on right-handed quarks to remove Y32Y_{32} can simultaneously generate Y12,22Y_{12,22} from Y13,23Y_{13,23}, giving

s12d=−s13ds23dors12u=−s13us23u.s^{d}_{12}\;=\;-\frac{s^{d}_{13}}{s^{d}_{23}}\qquad{\rm or}\qquad s^{u}_{12}\;=\;-\frac{s^{u}_{13}}{s^{u}_{23}}. (S35)

which lead to the results (S32) and (S33), with s12u≃0s^{u}_{12}\simeq 0 and s12d≃0s^{d}_{12}\simeq 0 in the results for β\beta and γ\gamma, respectively. Again, one angle of the unitarity triangle is given by the phase φ\varphi, so these textures also populate the peaks of Fig. 3. If Y12,23d=0Y^{d}_{12,23}=0, a rotation on right-handed quarks to remove Y32dY^{d}_{32} can simultaneously generate Y12,23dY^{d}_{12,23} from Y13,22dY^{d}_{13,22}, giving

s12d≃−s23d​s13d​(ybys)2,s23u≠0.s_{12}^{d}\simeq-s_{23}^{d}s^{d}_{13}\left(\frac{y_{b}}{y_{s}}\right)^{2},\qquad s^{u}_{23}\neq 0. (S36)

These textures populate the peak near π/4\pi/4 in Fig.  3. It is an accident that φ\varphi is near a multiple of π/8\pi/8; as yb/ysy_{b}/y_{s} deviates from the observed value, the peak in φ\varphi moves away from π/4\pi/4, as we show in App. V.a. A similar relation with up and down sectors interchanged is not realistic.

For hierarchical Yukawa matrices with 9-link textures, the only realistic relations between si​ju,ds^{u,d}_{ij} are given by (S35) and (S36). For (S36) there is no connection between φ\varphi and (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma), which are accidentally close to multiples of π/8\pi/8. However, all other textures lead to (S34) or (S35) at leading order requiring one of (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) to be equal to the rephasing-invariant angle φ\varphi. This explains both the peaks in Fig. 3 and the absence of textures between the peaks.

II.a Beyond 9-link textures: numerical sensitivity

Having established that, at leading order, all 9-link textures, apart from those with φ\varphi near π/4\pi/4, require one of the unitarity-triangle angles (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) to coincide with the rephasing-invariant phase φ\varphi, we now ask how robust this prediction is under the addition of further non-vanishing Yukawa entries. More precisely, we would like to understand how many zeros can be removed while preserving the predictions α≃π/2\alpha\simeq\pi/2, β≃π/8\beta\simeq\pi/8, or γ≃3​π/8\gamma\simeq 3\pi/8 as genuine consequences of the texture, rather than accidental numerical coincidences. We illustrate the general idea by analyzing the texture shown in Fig. 2 of the main text. We begin with the corresponding 9-link texture, fixing its non-vanishing entries to the values obtained from the fit to quark masses and CKM observables, and the rephasing invariant phase to π/2\pi/2. This texture predicts α≃π/2\alpha\simeq\pi/2 at leading order. We then switch on the vanishing entries, one by one, at their expected hierarchical size, Yi​ju/d∼ϵiq​ϵjuc/dcY^{u/d}_{ij}\sim\sqrt{\epsilon_{i}^{q}\,\epsilon_{j}^{u^{c}/d^{c}}}, where the ϵ\epsilon’s denote the U​(1)9U(1)^{9} spurions, and compute the numerical derivative of α\alpha,

limε→0α[Yu/di​j=εϵiq​ϵjuc/dc]−α[Yu/di​j=0]ε.\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\frac{\alpha\!\left[Y^{u/d}_{ij}=\varepsilon\sqrt{\epsilon_{i}^{q}\,\epsilon_{j}^{u^{c}/d^{c}}}\right]-\alpha\!\left[Y^{u/d}_{ij}=0\right]}{\varepsilon}. (S37)

Turning on a previously vanishing entry introduces an additional rephasing invariant into the theory. Consequently, the shift in α\alpha depends not only on the magnitude of the new Yukawa entry but also on its phase. To account for this dependence, we evaluate the derivative above for Yi​jY_{ij} taken to be purely real or purely imaginary, with both positive and negative signs, and retain the smallest value in each case.

The results are presented in Fig. S2. Each zero entry of the texture is assigned two numbers: the smallest derivative obtained for a purely imaginary perturbation (top) and for a purely real perturbation (bottom), both expressed in degrees. It is immediately apparent that three entries, Y13uY^{u}_{13}, Y13dY^{d}_{13}, and Y32dY^{d}_{32}, must be suppressed by one to two orders of magnitude with respect to their natural values, independently of their phase, in order to preserve the prediction α≃π/2\alpha\simeq\pi/2 at the level of one degree. The same conclusion applies to Y11dY^{d}_{11} when the perturbation is purely real, and to Y21uY^{u}_{21} when it is purely imaginary, once the projected LHCb precision with 300​fb−1300\,\mathrm{fb}^{-1} for β\beta and γ\gamma and the assumption of CKM unitarity is taken into account (see Tab. S1).

We checked that similar conclusions hold for several other textures, and in particular all the nine classes with φ=π/2\varphi=\pi/2 in Fig. 4. This is consistent with the expectation that, as the number of texture zeros decreases, the unitarity triangle angles receive multiple leading-order contributions, generally carrying different phases. Overall, this analysis indicates that at least four texture zeros are required to ensure that the relation between the unitarity-triangle angles and the rephasing-invariant phase is a genuine prediction of the texture, rather than an accidental numerical coincidence.

III Perturbative diagonalization

In this appendix, we explicitly examine three representative theories, where at leading order α\alpha, β\beta and γ\gamma, respectively, are the argument of a single rephasing invariant monomial. We perturbatively diagonalize the Yukawa matrices, parameterizing each entry as a power of a small parameter ϵ\epsilon (informed by the numerical fit), and compute the leading and subleading corrections to the unitarity angles. Since the parameters of the theory are determined by a fit to the physical observables, these corrections are necessarily expressible in terms of CKM matrix elements and quark masses.

Example I

First of all, we analyze a texture with φ=π/2\varphi=\pi/2. The Yukawa matrices are

Yu=(0i​u12​ϵ40u21​ϵ5u22​ϵ3000u33),Yd=(0d12​ϵ50d21​ϵ5d22​ϵ4d23​ϵ300d33​ϵ2)\displaystyle\begin{split}Y_{u}=\begin{pmatrix}0&i\,u_{12}\,\epsilon^{4}&0\\ u_{21}\,\epsilon^{5}&u_{22}\,\epsilon^{3}&0\\ 0&0&u_{33}\\ \end{pmatrix}\,,\quad Y_{d}=\begin{pmatrix}0&d_{12}\,\epsilon^{5}&0\\ d_{21}\,\epsilon^{5}&d_{22}\,\epsilon^{4}&d_{23}\,\epsilon^{3}\\ 0&0&d_{33}\,\epsilon^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\end{split} (S38)

where ϵ∼0.1\epsilon\sim 0.1 so that all the ui​ju_{ij} and di​jd_{ij} are 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1) numbers. where s12d≃−d12/d22ϵs_{12}^{d}\simeq-d_{12}/d_{22}\,\epsilon and s23d≃−d23/d33ϵs_{23}^{d}\simeq-d_{23}/d_{33}\,\epsilon. VCKM=VLuVLd†≃(1−s12d+s12u−s12u​s23ds12d−s12u∗1−s23ds12d​s23ds23d1).\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{\rm CKM}=V_{L}^{u}V_{L}^{d\,\dagger}\simeq\begin{pmatrix}1&-s_{12}^{d}+s_{12}^{u}&-s_{12}^{u}\,s_{23}^{d}\\ s_{12}^{d}-s_{12}^{u\,*}&1&-s_{23}^{d}\\ s_{12}^{d}\,s_{23}^{d}&s_{23}^{d}&1\\ \end{pmatrix}\,.\end{split} (S40)

Therefore, at leading order Vu​d,Vt​dV_{ud},V_{td} and Vt​bV_{tb} are real, while Vu​bV_{ub} is purely imaginary and α=arg(−Vt​dVt​b∗/Vu​dVu​b∗)=90∘\alpha={\rm arg}(-V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}/V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*})=90^{\circ}. The CKM elements and quark yukawas at leading order in ϵ\epsilon are

Vu​d≃Vc​s≃Vt​b≃1+𝒪(ϵ2),Vu​s=ϵ(d12d22−iu12u22)+𝒪(ϵ3),Vu​b=−iϵ2d23​u12d33​u22+𝒪(ϵ4),Vc​d=ϵ(−d12d22−iu12u22)+𝒪(ϵ3),Vc​b=ϵd23d33+𝒪(ϵ3),Vt​d=ϵ2d12​d23d33​d22+𝒪(ϵ4),Vt​s=−ϵd23d33+𝒪(ϵ3),yu2≃ϵ12u122​u212u222,yc2≃ϵ6u222,yt2≃u332,yd2≃ϵ12d122​d212d222,ys2≃ϵ8d222,yb2≃ϵ4d332.\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{ud}&\simeq V_{cs}\simeq V_{tb}\simeq 1+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\,,\;V_{us}=\epsilon\bigg(\frac{d_{12}}{d_{22}}-i\,\frac{u_{12}}{u_{22}}\bigg)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{ub}=-i\,\epsilon^{2}\,\frac{d_{23}u_{12}}{d_{33}u_{22}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\\ V_{cd}&=\epsilon\bigg(-\frac{d_{12}}{d_{22}}-i\,\frac{u_{12}}{u_{22}}\bigg)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{cb}=\epsilon\frac{d_{23}}{d_{33}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{td}=\epsilon^{2}\,\frac{d_{12}d_{23}}{d_{33}d_{22}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\;V_{ts}=-\epsilon\frac{d_{23}}{d_{33}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\\ y_{u}^{2}&\simeq\epsilon^{12}\frac{u_{12}^{2}u_{21}^{2}}{u_{22}^{2}}\,,\;y_{c}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{6}u_{22}^{2}\,,\;y_{t}^{2}\simeq u_{33}^{2}\,,\;y_{d}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{12}\frac{d_{12}^{2}d_{21}^{2}}{d_{22}^{2}}\,,\;y_{s}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{8}d_{22}^{2}\,,\;y_{b}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{4}d_{33}^{2}\,.\end{split} (S41)

To compute the next-to-leading order correction to α\alpha, we need higher order corrections to the CKM elements. We find

Vu​d=1−ϵ2(d1222​d222+u1222​u222−i​u12​d12d22​u22)+𝒪(ϵ3),Vu​b=−iϵ2d32​u12d33​u22+iϵ4d23​u12​(d332​u122+d232​u222)2​d333​u223+𝒪(ϵ5),Vt​d=ϵ2d12​d23d33​d22−ϵ4d23​d12​(d122+2​d212)2​d223​d33+𝒪(ϵ3),Vt​b=1−ϵ2d2322​d332+𝒪(ϵ5),α=arg⁡(−Vt​d​Vt​b∗Vu​d​Vu​b∗)≃arg⁡[i​d12​u22d22​u12+ϵ2​(d122d222+i​d12​d222​u122−d12​d212​u222d223​u12​u22)+𝒪⁡(ϵ3)]≃π2−d12​u12d22​u22​ϵ2+𝒪⁡(ϵ3)≃π2−|Vt​d​Vu​bVc​b​Vt​s|.\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{ud}&=1-\epsilon^{2}\bigg(\frac{d_{12}^{2}}{2d_{22}^{2}}+\frac{u_{12}^{2}}{2u_{22}^{2}}-\frac{i\,u_{12}d_{12}}{d_{22}u_{22}}\bigg)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{ub}=-i\,\epsilon^{2}\,\frac{d_{32}u_{12}}{d_{33}u_{22}}+i\,\epsilon^{4}\,\frac{d_{23}u_{12}(d_{33}^{2}u_{12}^{2}+d_{23}^{2}u_{22}^{2})}{2d_{33}^{3}u_{22}^{3}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{5})\,,\\ V_{td}&=\epsilon^{2}\,\frac{d_{12}d_{23}}{d_{33}d_{22}}-\epsilon^{4}\,\frac{d_{23}d_{12}(d_{12}^{2}+2d_{21}^{2})}{2d_{22}^{3}d_{33}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{tb}=1-\epsilon^{2}\frac{d_{23}^{2}}{2d_{33}^{2}}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{5})\,,\\ \alpha&=\arg\bigg(-\frac{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}\bigg)\simeq\arg\bigg[i\,\frac{d_{12}u_{22}}{d_{22}u_{12}}+\epsilon^{2}\bigg(\frac{d_{12}^{2}}{d_{22}^{2}}+i\,\frac{d_{12}d_{22}^{2}u_{12}^{2}-d_{12}d_{21}^{2}u_{22}^{2}}{d_{22}^{3}u_{12}u_{22}}\bigg)+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\bigg]\simeq\frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{d_{12}u_{12}}{d_{22}u_{22}}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\\ &\simeq\frac{\pi}{2}-\bigg|\frac{V_{td}\,V_{ub}}{V_{cb}\,V_{ts}}\bigg|\,.\end{split} (S42)

Example II

Now, we study a texture with φ=−π/8\varphi=-\pi/8. The Yukawa matrices are

Yu=(u11​ϵ50u13​ϵ20u22​ϵ2000u33),Yd=(d11​ϵ50d13​ϵ400d23​ϵ30d32​ϵ2ei​φ​d33​ϵ2),\displaystyle\begin{split}Y_{u}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{11}\,\epsilon^{5}&0&u_{13}\,\epsilon^{2}\\ 0&u_{22}\,\epsilon^{2}&0\\ 0&0&u_{33}\\ \end{pmatrix}\,,\quad Y_{d}=\begin{pmatrix}d_{11}\,\epsilon^{5}&0&d_{13}\,\epsilon^{4}\\ 0&0&d_{23}\,\epsilon^{3}\\ 0&d_{32}\epsilon^{2}&e^{i\varphi}\,d_{33}\,\epsilon^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\,,\end{split} (S43)

VLdV_{L}^{d} is well-approximated by VLd≃R12⋅R13⋅R23V_{L}^{d}\simeq R_{12}\cdot R_{13}\cdot R_{23}, with s23d≃−e−i​φd23d33/(d322+d332)ϵs^{d}_{23}\simeq\,-e^{-i\varphi}d_{23}d_{33}/(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})\,\epsilon, s13d≃−e−i​φd13d33/(d322+d332)ϵ2s^{d}_{13}\simeq\,-e^{-i\varphi}d_{13}d_{33}/(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})\,\epsilon^{2} and sd12=−d13/d23ϵs^{d}_{12}=-d_{13}/d_{23}\,\epsilon,

VLd≃(1s12ds13d+s12d​s23d−s12d1s23d−sd∗13−sd∗231).\displaystyle V^{d}_{L}\simeq\begin{pmatrix}1&s^{d}_{12}&s^{d}_{13}+s^{d}_{12}s^{d}_{23}\\[5.69054pt] -s^{d}_{12}&1&s^{d}_{23}\\[5.69054pt] -s^{d\,*}_{13}&-s^{d\,*}_{23}&1\end{pmatrix}\,. (S44)

VLuV_{L}^{u} is an exact 11-33 rotation, with su13≃−u13/u33ϵ2s^{u}_{13}\simeq-u_{13}/u_{33}\,\epsilon^{2}. The CKM elements and quark Yukawas at leading order are

Vu​d≃Vc​s≃Vt​b≃1+𝒪(ϵ2),Vu​s=d13d23ϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vu​b=[d13​d33d322+d332ei​φ−u13u33]ϵ2+𝒪(ϵ4),Vc​d=−d13d33ϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vc​b=d23​d33d322+d332ei​φϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vt​s=−d23​d33d322+d332e−i​φϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vt​d=u13u33ϵ2+𝒪(ϵ4),yu2≃ϵ10u112,yc2≃ϵ4u222,yt2≃u332,yd2≃ϵ10d112,ys2≃ϵ6d232​d322d322+d332,yb2≃ϵ4(d322+d332).\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{ud}&\simeq V_{cs}\simeq V_{tb}\simeq 1+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\,,\;V_{us}=\frac{d_{13}}{d_{23}}\,\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{ub}=\bigg[\,\frac{d_{13}d_{33}}{d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2}}e^{i\varphi}-\frac{u_{13}}{u_{33}}\,\bigg]\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\\[5.69054pt] V_{cd}&=-\frac{d_{13}}{d_{33}}\,\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{cb}=\frac{d_{23}d_{33}}{d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2}}e^{i\varphi}\,\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{ts}=-\frac{d_{23}d_{33}}{d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2}}e^{-i\varphi}\,\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{td}=\frac{u_{13}}{u_{33}}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\\[5.69054pt] y_{u}^{2}&\simeq\epsilon^{10}\,u_{11}^{2}\,,\;y_{c}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{4}\,u_{22}^{2}\,,\;y_{t}^{2}\simeq u_{33}^{2}\,,\;y_{d}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{10}\,d_{11}^{2}\,,\;y_{s}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{6}\,\frac{d_{23}^{2}d_{32}^{2}}{d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2}}\,,\;y_{b}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{4}\,(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})\,.\end{split} (S45)

so that,

β=arg⁡(−Vc​d​Vc​b∗Vt​d​Vt​b∗)=arg⁡(d13​d33​u33(d322+d332)​u13​e−i​φ)≃−φ.\displaystyle\beta={\rm arg}\!\left(-\frac{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}\right)={\rm arg}\!\left(\frac{d_{13}d_{33}u_{33}}{(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})u_{13}}e^{-i\varphi}\right)\simeq-\varphi\,. (S46)

For φ=−π/8\varphi=-\pi/8 we get β≃π/8\beta\simeq\pi/8, in agreement with the experimental measurement. At next-to-leading order, we find

Vt​b=1−d232​d3322​(d322+d332)2ϵ2+𝒪(ϵ4),Vc​b=−d23​d33d322+d332ei​φϵ+d233​d33∗(2​d322−d332)2​(d322+d332)3ei​φϵ3+𝒪(ϵ5),Vc​d=−d13d23ϵ+[d1332​d233−d13​d23​d3322​(d322+d332)2]ϵ3+𝒪(ϵ5),Vt​d=u13u33ϵ2+[d13​d232​d33(d322+d332)2e−i​φ−u13​d1322​u33​d232]ϵ4+𝒪(ϵ6),β=arg⁡(−Vc​d​Vc​b∗Vt​d​Vt​b∗)=arg⁡([d13​d33​u33u13​(d322+d332)+𝒪⁡(ϵ2)]​e−i​φ−d132​d232​d332​u332u132​(d322+d332)3​e−i​2​φ​ϵ2+𝒪⁡(ϵ3))≃π8−12​2−2​d13​d232​d33​u33(d322+d332)2​u13​ϵ2≃π8−12​2−2​|Vu​sVt​d​ys2yb2|.\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{tb}&=1-\frac{d_{23}^{2}d_{33}^{2}}{2(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})^{2}}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\quad\;V_{cb}=-\frac{d_{23}d_{33}}{d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2}}e^{i\varphi}\,\epsilon+\frac{d_{23}^{3}d_{33}*(2d_{32}^{2}-d_{33}^{2})}{2(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})^{3}}e^{i\varphi}\epsilon^{3}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{5})\,,\\[5.69054pt] V_{cd}&=-\frac{d_{13}}{d_{23}}\,\epsilon+\bigg[\frac{d_{13}^{3}}{2d_{23}^{3}}-\frac{d_{13}\,d_{23}\,d_{33}^{2}}{2(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})^{2}}\bigg]\epsilon^{3}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{5})\;,\quad\;V_{td}=\frac{u_{13}}{u_{33}}\epsilon^{2}+\bigg[\frac{d_{13}d_{23}^{2}d_{33}}{(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})^{2}}e^{-i\varphi}-\frac{u_{13}d_{13}^{2}}{2u_{33}d_{23}^{2}}\bigg]\epsilon^{4}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{6})\,,\\[5.69054pt] \beta&={\rm arg}\!\left(-\frac{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}{V_{td}V_{tb}^{*}}\right)={\rm arg}\!\left(\bigg[\frac{d_{13}\,d_{33}\,u_{33}}{u_{13}(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\bigg]\,e^{-i\varphi}-\frac{d_{13}^{2}d_{23}^{2}d_{33}^{2}u_{33}^{2}}{u_{13}^{2}(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})^{3}}\,e^{-i2\varphi}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\right)\\ &\simeq\frac{\pi}{8}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2}}\frac{d_{13}d_{23}^{2}d_{33}u_{33}}{(d_{32}^{2}+d_{33}^{2})^{2}u_{13}}\epsilon^{2}\simeq\frac{\pi}{8}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2-\sqrt{2}}\bigg|\frac{V_{us}}{V_{td}}\frac{y_{s}^{2}}{y_{b}^{2}}\bigg|.\end{split} (S47)

Example III

Finally, we analyze a pair of textures with φ=5​π/8\varphi=5\pi/8. The Yukawa matrices are

Yu=(u11​ϵ5000u22​ϵ2u23​ϵ00u33),Yd=(0ei​φ​d12​ϵ4d13​ϵ40d22​ϵ30d31​ϵ30d33​ϵ2).\displaystyle\begin{split}Y_{u}=\begin{pmatrix}u_{11}\epsilon^{5}&0&0\\ 0&u_{22}\,\epsilon^{2}&u_{23}\,\epsilon\\ 0&0&u_{33}\\ \end{pmatrix}\,,\quad Y_{d}=\begin{pmatrix}0&e^{i\varphi}d_{12}\,\epsilon^{4}&d_{13}\epsilon^{4}\\ 0&d_{22}\,\epsilon^{3}&0\\ d_{31}\epsilon^{3}&0&d_{33}\,\epsilon^{2}\\ \end{pmatrix}\,.\end{split} (S48)

VLdV_{L}^{d} is well-approximated by the product of a 11-33 and a 11-22 rotation, VLd≃R12⋅R13V_{L}^{d}\simeq R_{12}\cdot R_{13}, with sd13≃−d13/d33ϵ2s^{d}_{13}\simeq-d_{13}/d_{33}\,\epsilon^{2} and sd12=−ei​φd12/d22ϵs^{d}_{12}=-e^{i\varphi}d_{12}/d_{22}\,\epsilon

VLd≃(1−s12ds13d−sd∗121−sd13sd∗12−su∗1301).\displaystyle V^{d}_{L}\simeq\begin{pmatrix}1&-s^{d}_{12}&s^{d}_{13}\\[5.69054pt] -s^{d\,*}_{12}&1&-s^{d}_{13}s^{d\,*}_{12}\\[5.69054pt] -s^{u\,*}_{13}&0&1\end{pmatrix}\,. (S49)

VLuV_{L}^{u} is an exact 22-33 rotation, with su23≃−u23/u33ϵs^{u}_{23}\simeq-u_{23}/u_{33}\epsilon. The CKM elements and quark Yukawas at leading order are

Vu​d≃Vc​s≃Vt​b≃1+𝒪(ϵ2),Vu​s=d12d22e−i​φϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vu​b=d13d33ϵ2+𝒪(ϵ4),Vc​d=−d12d22ei​φϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vc​b=−u23u33ϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vt​s=u23u33ϵ+𝒪(ϵ3),Vt​d=−u23​d12u33​d22ei​φϵ2−d13d33ϵ2+𝒪(ϵ4),yu2≃ϵ10u112,yc2≃ϵ4u222,yt2≃u332,yd2≃ϵ10d132​d312d332,ys2≃ϵ6d222,yb2≃ϵ4d332.\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{ud}&\simeq V_{cs}\simeq V_{tb}\simeq 1+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{2})\,,\;V_{us}=\frac{d_{12}}{d_{22}}\,e^{-i\varphi}\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{ub}=\frac{d_{13}}{d_{33}}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\\ V_{cd}&=-\frac{d_{12}}{d_{22}}\,e^{i\varphi}\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{cb}=-\frac{u_{23}}{u_{33}}\,\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{ts}=\frac{u_{23}}{u_{33}}\,\epsilon+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{3})\,,\;V_{td}=-\frac{u_{23}d_{12}}{u_{33}d_{22}}e^{i\varphi}\epsilon^{2}-\frac{d_{13}}{d_{33}}\epsilon^{2}+\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\\ y_{u}^{2}&\simeq\epsilon^{10}\,u_{11}^{2}\,,\;y_{c}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{4}\,u_{22}^{2}\,,\;y_{t}^{2}\simeq u_{33}^{2}\,,\;y_{d}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{10}\,\frac{d_{13}^{2}d_{31}^{2}}{d_{33}^{2}}\,,\;y_{s}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{6}\,d_{22}^{2}\,,\;y_{b}^{2}\simeq\epsilon^{4}\,d_{33}^{2}\,.\end{split} (S50)

Here Vu​bV_{ub} and Vc​bV_{cb} are real while Vu​sV_{us} and Vc​dV_{cd} carry the CP phase, so φ\varphi lands in the ratio Vu​d​Vu​b∗/Vc​d​Vc​b∗V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}/V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*} and hence in γ\gamma. At leading order,

γ=arg⁡(−Vu​d​Vu​b∗Vc​d​Vc​b∗)=arg⁡(−d13​d22​u33u23​d33​d12​e−i​φ)≃π−φ.\displaystyle\gamma={\rm arg}\!\left(-\frac{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}\right)={\rm arg}\!\left(-\frac{d_{13}\,d_{22}u_{33}}{u_{23}\,d_{33}\,d_{12}}\,e^{-i\varphi}\right)\simeq\pi-\varphi\,. (S51)

For φ=5​π/8\varphi=5\pi/8, we get γ≃3​π/8\gamma\simeq 3\pi/8, in agreement with experiments. At next-to-leading order we obtain

Vu​d=1−d1222​d222ϵ2+𝒪(ϵ4),Vc​d=−d12d22ei​φ[ϵ−u2322​u332ϵ3−d1222​d222ϵ3]+u23​d13u33​d33ϵ3+𝒪(ϵ5),Vu​b=d13d33ϵ2+d13​d312d333ϵ4+𝒪(ϵ6),Vc​b=−u23u33ϵ+u2332​u333ϵ3+𝒪(ϵ5).γ=arg⁡(−Vu​d​Vu​b∗Vc​d​Vc​b∗)=arg⁡(−d13​d22​u33d12​d33​u23​e−i​φ−d222​d132d122​d332​e−i​2​φ​ϵ2)≃3​π8−12​2+2​d22​d13​u23d12​d33​u33​ϵ2≃3​π8−12​2+2​|Vc​b​Vu​bVu​s|.\displaystyle\begin{split}V_{ud}&=1\;-\;\frac{d_{12}^{2}}{2\,d_{22}^{2}}\,\epsilon^{2}\;+\;\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{4})\,,\quad\quad\quad\quad V_{cd}=-\frac{d_{12}}{d_{22}}\,e^{i\varphi}\Bigl[\epsilon-\frac{u_{23}^{2}}{2\,u_{33}^{2}}\epsilon^{3}-\frac{d_{12}^{2}}{2\,d_{22}^{2}}\epsilon^{3}\,\Bigr]+\frac{u_{23}d_{13}}{u_{33}d_{33}}\epsilon^{3}+\;\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{5})\,,\\[5.69054pt] V_{ub}&=\frac{d_{13}}{d_{33}}\,\epsilon^{2}+\frac{d_{13}d_{31}^{2}}{d_{33}^{3}}\epsilon^{4}\;+\;\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{6})\,,\quad\quad V_{cb}=-\frac{u_{23}}{u_{33}}\,\epsilon\;+\;\frac{u_{23}^{3}}{2\,u_{33}^{3}}\,\epsilon^{3}\,+\;\mathcal{O}(\epsilon^{5})\,.\\[5.69054pt] \gamma&={\rm arg}\!\left(-\frac{V_{ud}V_{ub}^{*}}{V_{cd}V_{cb}^{*}}\right)={\rm arg}\!\left(-\frac{d_{13}\,d_{22}u_{33}}{d_{12}\,d_{33}\,u_{23}}\,e^{-i\varphi}-\frac{d_{22}^{2}d_{13}^{2}}{d_{12}^{2}d_{33}^{2}}\,e^{-i2\varphi}\epsilon^{2}\right)\simeq\frac{3\pi}{8}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}\,\frac{d_{22}d_{13}u_{23}}{d_{12}d_{33}u_{33}}\epsilon^{2}\\ &\simeq\,\frac{3\pi}{8}-\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2+\sqrt{2}}\,\bigg|\frac{V_{cb}\,V_{ub}}{V_{us}}\bigg|.\end{split} (S52)

IV The π/4\pi/4 peak

As already mentioned in Sec. II, while the {π/2,π/8,3​π/8}\{\pi/2,\pi/8,3\pi/8\} values of the rephasing invariant phase in the 9-link textures have a simple explanation in terms of their connection to the angles of the unitarity triangle, the same is not true for the π/4\pi/4 peak, which is related to a coincidence at the level of the quark masses. In this section, we focus on a particular example of a texture where φ=π/4\varphi=\pi/4 is needed to reproduce the data,
